name: Motivational interviewing
heroTitle: Understand the hesitation before forcing a decision.
summary: Motivational interviewing helps explore mixed feelings about change. Learn how collaboration, careful listening, and your own reasons differ from persuasion, pressure, or a therapist choosing for you.
panelParagraphs: Wanting change and fearing its costs can happen at the same time. The conversation makes room for both, while helping you hear your own priorities more clearly.

model.title: A guiding conversation, not a sales pitch for change.
paragraphs: Motivational interviewing is a collaborative communication approach that pays particular attention to a person's own reasons for change. It sits between simply directing someone and following without a focus. The practitioner listens for values, concerns, hopes, and uncertainty while respecting the person's autonomy.

Ambivalence means having competing motivations. A habit may cause problems and still provide relief, belonging, predictability, or something else important. Arguing only for change can miss what the person fears losing. A useful conversation explores those meanings instead of treating hesitation as a character flaw.

MI can be used within different services and therapies. It is not, by itself, a complete treatment plan for every concern. Information, assessment, specialist treatment, practical support, and a concrete plan may also be needed.

panel.title: Your reasons should be recognizable as yours.
paragraphs: A clinician can offer information with permission and raise concerns honestly. The process should not disguise the clinician's preferred choice as something you have independently decided.

example.title: Less evening scrolling sounds good. Giving it up does not.
example.intro: A fictional example of a low-stakes behavior change, not a guide to changing a substance-use pattern.

items.title: Reasons to change
paragraphs: Avery wants more sleep and feels frustrated about losing an evening to a phone. They imagine being more present with family and less tired in the morning.

items.title: Reasons to keep things as they are
paragraphs: The phone is also a way to decompress after a demanding day. Avery worries that giving it up would leave them with chores, tension, and no time that feels their own.

items.title: A more useful focus
paragraphs: The conversation shifts from proving that scrolling is bad to understanding rest, choice, connection, and what Avery would be willing to try.

reveal.title: What might the clinician do instead of persuading?
paragraphs: A clinician could reflect both sides accurately and ask what matters most to Avery about a different evening. Avery may decide that the first priority is protecting actual downtime, not enforcing a stricter rule. Any plan would then need to address that priority instead of taking away the only available break.

This is a fictional illustration of autonomy and ambivalence. It does not imply that every habit can be changed safely without assessment or that a small experiment is the right response to a medically risky situation.

toolsTitle: The skills support a relationship, not a persuasion technique.
toolsIntro: Open questions, reflections, affirmations, and summaries are useful when they serve genuine understanding.

tools.title: Open questions
tools.teaser: Invite detail that a yes-or-no answer may miss.
paragraphs: A question can explore what change would mean, what feels difficult, or what a person has already considered. Its value lies in the answer, not in steering the person toward an expected response.
A rapid series of questions can feel like an interview rather than collaboration. Listening between questions is part of the work.

tools.title: Reflective listening
tools.teaser: Check the meaning instead of immediately correcting it.
paragraphs: A reflection offers the clinician's understanding of what was said, including the tension between different wishes. The person can correct it. Good reflection is not simply repeating words or agreeing with everything.
It can make ambivalence easier to hear without arguing either side into silence.

tools.title: Your language about change
tools.teaser: Explore desire, ability, reasons, need, and readiness.
paragraphs: A clinician may notice statements that point toward change and invite elaboration. They also attend to concerns about maintaining the current pattern. The aim is not to collect the right phrases as proof of compliance.
A person's readiness can differ from the importance of the goal or their confidence that change is possible.

tools.title: Planning when it fits
tools.teaser: Turn a decision into a realistic next step, without rushing it.
paragraphs: When a person is ready, the conversation can move toward options and a plan. Permission-based information and shared consideration of barriers can help connect intention with action.
A premature plan may bypass the very uncertainty that needs attention. Not every useful session ends with a commitment.

processTitle: Four overlapping tasks in an MI-informed conversation.

process.title: Engage
paragraphs: Develop enough understanding and trust to work together. The person should feel heard rather than managed.

process.title: Focus
paragraphs: Agree on what the conversation is about. A shared focus is different from a hidden agenda.

process.title: Evoke
paragraphs: Explore the person's own motivations, values, and concerns. Their reasons matter more than a persuasive lecture.

process.title: Plan
paragraphs: When appropriate, consider a next step that reflects readiness, resources, and barriers. The process can return to earlier tasks as needed.

limitsTitle: Respecting autonomy and addressing risk can coexist.

limits.title: Not manipulation
paragraphs: MI should not be used to obtain an answer the clinician has already decided is correct. Honest discussion of risks and professional recommendations is different from covert pressure.

limits.title: Not sufficient for every treatment need
paragraphs: A collaborative conversation does not replace medical evaluation, crisis care, or a specialized treatment when those are indicated. In particular, changing some substance-use patterns can involve medical risks that require assessment.

questions.question: Does this mean the therapist never gives advice?
paragraphs: Not necessarily. Information and recommendations can be offered openly and with permission, with attention to what you understand and what matters to you. MI is not withholding useful knowledge; it is avoiding a tug-of-war over your choices.

questions.question: What if I decide not to change?
paragraphs: Your autonomy remains important. The clinician may still discuss concerns or limitations of the service honestly. A session can clarify a decision without manufacturing commitment.

questions.question: Is MI only used for addiction?
paragraphs: No. It is used in a range of behavior-change conversations. Its use in a setting does not make it a complete treatment for every issue in that setting. Ask how it fits the overall plan.

questions.question: How is it different from solution-focused therapy?
paragraphs: MI particularly attends to motivation and ambivalence about change. [Solution-focused therapy](/solution-focused-brief-therapy/) emphasizes a preferred future, exceptions, and useful differences. Both can be collaborative, but their focal questions are not identical.

questions.question: Will every session end with homework?
paragraphs: No. Planning should fit readiness and purpose. Sometimes the meaningful work is clarifying why a change matters, what it might cost, or what support would make it feasible.
